note: Every enquiry this archive has sent, what came back, and what is still owed. It existed in three places — prose on the open-questions page, entries in the research log, and drafts in a folder — and no one of them showed what was outstanding. Reconstructing it took a search of an inbox rather than a look at this site, which is the failure this page is here to stop.

rows.what: Six Transvaal estate files — TAB MHG 1095/48, 3734/46, 769/52, 5155/51, 10/57 and 52653
rows.back: 15 September, Ms Mavis Xaba, Reading Room: “ALL THE ESTATE FILES YOU ARE REQUESTING ARE BOUND FILES. Unfortunately, we are therefore unable to scan these files and provide complete digital copies by email.” Not a refusal — a physical fact about the record. She corrected none of the six references and put a private researcher on copy.

rows.what: The same six bound estate files — what she charges and how, her own view of whether the work is worth doing, and an offer to begin with one
rows.back: THE FIRST PAID-RESEARCH APPROACH THIS PROJECT HAS MADE. Everything before it went to an institution and waited. No payment details were sent and none will be: the letter asks her to name her own arrangement.

DELIBERATELY NOT SENT. The National Archives' own record gives pmbarchives@dact.kzntl.gov.za on an entry last touched in 2015 and kzntl.gov.za is a retired domain; other listings give pmbarchives@kzndac.gov.za. The postal address and the telephone agree everywhere. This archive has already posted one enquiry into a mailbox it could not confirm. 15 SEPTEMBER, AND THE REASON FOR HOLDING IT IS WEAKER THAN IT WAS: both domains ACCEPT MAIL. kzndac.gov.za and dact.kzntl.gov.za each have MX records and no website, which is an ordinary shape for a government department. A domain taking mail and a person reading the mailbox are different facts, so telephoning first is still the better plan — but “almost certainly dead” was more than the evidence supported.

rows.what: WO 97 and WO 12 for the 21st Light Dragoons — the discharge paper that would give James Mountjoy his parish of birth
rows.back: Raised 15 September, on one sentence in a newspaper. The first errand this archive has had outside South Africa. 15 SEPTEMBER — AND IT CANNOT BE POSTED AS AN EMAIL. The National Archives take records and research enquiries THROUGH A WEB FORM and publish no enquiry address; the domain has a mailbox but no address anybody is invited to write to. This archive does not send letters into mailboxes it cannot confirm — it has said so about Pietermaritzburg for two days and will not make an exception for itself. The letter is written and waiting on a decision about the form.

rows.what: Guidance on tracing James Mountjoy, a saddler discharged from the 21st Dragoons (Light) at the Cape in 1816 or 1817 — which series after WO 97, and whether WO 12/1430 is the musters to read
rows.back: DRAFTED AFTER SEARCHING, NOT INSTEAD OF IT. Discovery was searched for four spellings across the WO series: the name-catalogued discharge series hold two Montjoys and neither is this man. The control says the absence is real — 95 WO 97 records for “21st Dragoons (Light)” in a single page — so the letter asks whether the reading is right (pensioners' papers would not hold a man discharged at the Cape without a pension) and points at WO 12/1430 and the WO 25 description books. 15 SEPTEMBER — AND IT CANNOT BE POSTED AS AN EMAIL. The National Archives take records and research enquiries THROUGH A WEB FORM and publish no enquiry address; the domain has a mailbox but no address anybody is invited to write to. This archive does not send letters into mailboxes it cannot confirm — it has said so about Pietermaritzburg for two days and will not make an exception for itself. The letter is written and waiting on a decision about the form. ··· CORRECTED 17 SEPTEMBER, BEFORE POSTING. The draft named WO 12/1430 as the piece to read. THAT IS THE 20TH AND 21ST DRAGOONS FOR 1867–1868 — fifty years late and the re-raised regiment. The 21st Light Dragoons has its own run and the piece is WO 12/1450, 1816–1817. The draft now names it, gives the newspaper evidence for a SEPTEMBER 1817 departure, and tells them plainly that an earlier version had the wrong piece.

rows.to: National Library of South Africa, Special Collections, Cape Town
rows.what: MSB751, the GA Kolbe Collection — a copy of the letter of 23 August 1830 from Johan Kolbe in London to his son — described by the catalogue as written on his ordination, which it was not, and whether it carries a London address
rows.back: SENT 15 September to specialcollections@nlsa.ac.za, after checking that the domain takes mail. A DIFFERENT BUILDING FROM THE ONE THIS ARCHIVE KEEPS WRITING TO: the library at 5 Queen Victoria Street, not the archives at 72 Roeland Street. It asks for the letter of 23 August 1830, for whether it carries a London address at its head, and for two things about the item itself — where the original is, since the catalogue calls this a photocopy, and whether “LMS missionary” comes from the papers or from the donor. THAT LAST QUESTION IS THE ONE THAT MATTERS MOST: the only other evidence for his mission work is a recollection written down forty-five years later, and whether the two are independent witnesses or one family memory told twice is the difference between corroboration and an echo. ··· ANSWERED IN TWENTY-THREE HOURS, 16 SEPTEMBER, BY MELANIE GEUSTYN. “I have placed a request for the George Augustus Kolbe manuscript to be retrieved. THE MANUSCRIPT COLLECTIONS ARE KEPT IN OFF-SITE VAULTS, and it should get to my desk after 11:00 tomorrow. I HAVE ALSO ASKED THAT THE BACKGROUND FILE ON THE COLLECTION BE RETRIEVED FOR ME — hopefully there might be additional information regarding the donation there. Once I have these items at hand, I will be able to assist in answering your questions.” NO ANSWERS YET AND TWO THINGS ALREADY GAINED. The manuscript is not lost, not missing and not unfindable — it is in a vault and somebody has sent for it. AND THERE IS A BACKGROUND FILE, which this archive did not know existed: the library’s own paperwork on the 1985 donation, which is where an answer to “where is the original” and “who was Dr Jean Griffiths” would live if it lives anywhere. NOTHING TO REPLY TO YET; she has not asked a question and has said she will come back. ··· AND ON 18 SEPTEMBER THE DOCUMENT ITSELF ARRIVED — THREE DAYS AFTER THE ENQUIRY WENT IN. Melanie Geustyn sent the four-page manuscript and, unasked, a two-page DICTIONARY OF SOUTH AFRICAN BIOGRAPHY entry written by DR KAREL SCHOEMAN with a list of sources. THE LETTER DOES NOT CARRY A STREET ADDRESS — “London” and nothing finer — so the Brunswick Square question stands. IT DOES SETTLE THE OTHER ONE: the LMS acceptance is in the father’s own hand in 1830, independent of a memoir written forty-five years later. And it gives Henry’s dropsy, Elizabeth in Edinburgh, Charlotte by name, and the line that dates the obituary — “kind love from your SISTERS & BROTHER”. THE BACKGROUND FILE HOLDS NOTHING FURTHER on the donation or on Dr Griffiths, so the original cannot be traced from that end. [The letter](/documents/#msb751)

rows.to: Melanie Geustyn, Senior Librarian, Special Collections, National Library of South Africa
rows.what: A thank-you, telling her what MSB 751 produced — and two remaining questions: was the DSAB entry ever published, and did the catalogue’s “LMS missionary” come from the papers or the donor
rows.back: DRAFTED 20 September, NOT SENT; the sending is David’s. It goes as a REPLY to her email of 18 September so it keeps the thread and the MSB 751 reference. THE ENQUIRY WENT IN ON 15 SEPTEMBER AND WAS ANSWERED ON THE 18TH — three days, the whole manuscript scanned, and a second document nobody had asked for. A special-collections librarian rarely learns what a request was for or whether it came to anything; this one came to a great deal. The letter says what it settled (the LMS acceptance in the father’s own hand, Henry dying of dropsy, “sisters & brother” dating the obituary’s eight sons) AND WHAT IT DID NOT — the heading is “London” and nothing finer, so Brunswick Square against Conduit Street is still open. It also tells her the second attachment corrected this archive. ONE QUESTION ONLY, AND MARKED OPTIONAL: the typescript is unsigned, initialled and dated 18/2/92, and the Library is the only body that can say who wrote it and whether the entry was ever published. This archive would rather credit it than publish it as anonymous.

rows.to: Centre for Research Collections, University of Edinburgh
rows.what: CSWC 60 item 3 — a correction to the catalogue (Edinburgh calls Kolbe “a moravian missionary?”; he was LMS) and a request for a reproduction
rows.back: DRAFTED, NOT SENT; the sending is David’s. **THE ONLY LETTER IN THIS FOLDER THAT GIVES BEFORE IT ASKS.** Edinburgh’s own description carries a question mark, so the cataloguer already doubted it; this archive can settle it with the NLSA catalogue of MSB 751 and with the father’s letter of 23 August 1830 — “fully accepted by the [L.M.S.] as one of their Missionaries” — and can add the service dates from the DSAB draft. It also tells Edinburgh what it appears not to know: the original watercolour is recorded in the Africana Museum, Johannesburg. THEN it asks for a copy of item 3, offers to pay the reproduction fee, and falls back on asking for the dimensions and any inscription if a scan is not straightforward. THIS ARCHIVE HOLDS NO LIKENESS OF ANYBODY BORN BEFORE 1850.

rows.what: The photocopy of the 1819 Kolbe–Downing marriage certificate named in the DSAB source list, and anything else filed under Kolbe or Owen’s party
rows.back: DRAFTED, NOT SENT; the sending is David’s. The Albany Museum holds A GENEALOGICAL ARCHIVE OF THE 1820 BRITISH SETTLERS, and he was one — Algoa Bay, 14 April 1820, the Nautilus, Owen’s party, entered as a chemist. The letter quotes the DSAB source line verbatim in Afrikaans, explains why the CERTIFICATE is not the ALLEGATION this archive already holds (witnesses and signatures, and the bride signed the allegation with a mark), offers to pay any fee, says plainly that David cannot visit and asks whether there is a research service. AND IT ASKS A SECOND QUESTION: anything else under KOLBE or under OWEN’S PARTY, because what this archive has of his first four years at the Cape is one sentence in a secondary work.

rows.what: Tell her the invoice cannot be paid before Tuesday, and let her choose between moving the visit and a reduced set
rows.back: DRAFTED 20 September, NOT SENT; the sending and the choice within it are David’s. **HE SAID ON THE 16TH THAT HE WOULD PAY STRAIGHT AWAY AND HE CANNOT.** Invoice No 463, R11,400 plus R200, against a visit to Pretoria on Tuesday 22 September for which she has already arranged the files. The letter does not haggle and does not go quiet. It says the payment will not arrive in time, says the misjudgement was the scope and not her pricing, and **puts the decision in her hands because it is her day that is booked**: move the visit to a date after payment, or keep Tuesday with a reduced set — with **TAB MHG 40293, the Kolbe death notice, SUBSTITUTED IN RATHER THAN ADDED**. It withdraws Groups A, B and C entirely so nothing is worked that is not on a paid invoice. **AND IT SAYS WHY SHE IS WORTH KEEPING**: she volunteered a cap on her own fees unasked and gave a seventh file free.

rows.to: Special Collections, SOAS Library — the Council for World Mission archive
rows.what: Copies of four journals of George Augustus Kolbe, 1828–1834, and the incoming correspondence for 1835–1837
rows.back: DRAFTED, NOT SENT; the sending is David’s. **THE MOST IMPORTANT LETTER IN THIS FOLDER, AND THE ONLY ONE THAT NAMES EVERY REFERENCE IT WANTS**, because the SOAS catalogue is item-level and all seven were found in two searches. FOUR JOURNALS IN HIS OWN HAND: CWM/LMS/05/05/100 (Melvill and Kolbe, tour north-east of Philippolis, 13–22 Nov 1828), /102 (1828–1831), /106 (1831–1834), /108 (6 Oct 1832 – Sep 1833). INCOMING CORRESPONDENCE: /044 (1835, which names him), /046 (1836) and the 1837 file, Box 15 — asked for with the reason stated plainly, that this archive would rather read what the Directors were told about the 1836 accusation than keep repeating a summary of it. It offers to start with one item. AND ONE QUESTION THAT NEEDS NO SEARCHING: whether candidate papers survive as a class, since Frederick William Kolbe’s would settle Sibree’s error outright. `special.collections@soas.ac.uk` — AND IT IS IN LONDON, the one archive on this list a person could walk into.
